title: AI shopping agents test trust as holiday gift season nears
excerpt: AI agents were poised to do a lot of holiday shopping this year, but retailers and customers aren't yet ready to trust the tech.
content_html:
The first agentic AI Black Friday is off to a rocky start

By Dominick Reuter

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-22T12:10:01.258Z

When Dean Mandelos wanted to find a holiday gift for his sister, he turned to his handy new personal AI agent, Muse.

The bot, which Meta launched in September, had already helped the 29-year-old therapist in New York City list and sell a few items on eBay. It had also dutifully gathered and organized multiple bids from contractors for a door replacement job, so he figured it might be useful in finding something unique for his sister who loves to cook. Muse recommended a set of knives.

"I think that it was giving some good ideas. I just think that the thing that AI consistently misses is, like, the social aspect," Mandelos said. "My first thought would have been that it would suggest a cookbook or something. But instead, it went right towards actual tools and equipment."

Beyond more utilitarian recommendations, Mandelos also said his Muse agent encountered other hiccups in its shopping journey, from listings that had expired or sold out, to outright blocks from major e-commerce sites like Amazon and eBay.

"I would like to let it do its own thing," he said. "I need to have a reason to trust it more."

This year is the first holiday season since the release of easy-to-use AI agents to the general public. While the tools can act like personal assistants for many, it remains to be seen whether people will actually trust them to handle the annual ritual of shopping for loved ones, a deeply personal experience for many.

Mandelos' experience highlights a conundrum: the use of AI agents collides with established habits of both retailers and shoppers. While an AI bot could handle many people's holiday gift lists, it may take time before bots are trusted and empowered to truly take on the job by both consumers and retailers.

"It's the first Black Friday that AI can really play a meaningful role for sure, but it's not fully autonomous yet," said Kantar retail analyst Gina Logan. "Two-thirds of shoppers are using AI for shopping at least sometimes, but over half still prefer to control their own shopping decisions."

Early and slow adoption

For all the fanfare from marketers about the arrival of agentic commerce, there's little evidence that shoppers are handing off checkout to bots.

A Bain & Co. analysis this week of Similarweb data found that AI assistants represent less than 1% of retailers' web traffic. DoorDash and Uber also recently said that very few of their customers are using agents. Of about 320 million Uber transactions in the final week of October, only about 500 were from AI agents.

That said, adoption is rising fast, and the Bain report finds AI search is almost twice as effective as traditional web search at ultimately converting to a sale.

Abhishek Bora, head of growth at streetwear retailer All Star Elite, told Business Insider that agentic traffic accounts for about 1% of his website traffic, mostly from Meta's Muse. It's also unclear to him whether those agents are actually making a purchase or simply finding items for customers to click "buy" on.

"Once a week or twice a week we get a Muse purchase," he said. "It's small, but we have been optimizing for it."

For Bora, that means adding machine-readable data layers to All Star Elite's website that help a bot better navigate and understand the products and promotions the company offers.

The 1% figure also appears in a survey from the consumer insights platform Zappi, which found that 1% of respondents mentioned — without prompting — that they use AI to shop.

Steve Phillips, the firm's founder and chief innovation officer, said these agentic one percenters generally skewed younger, wealthier, and more tech-savvy.

"That's not unusual for any sort of tech. They would be the first people buying Apple phones," he said.

Phillips likened the uptake of agentic shopping to the first days of booking hotels on the internet in the early dot-com era. Travelers would search the web for a room and then pick up the phone to make a reservation.

"No one was booking online, but people were using the web, and I think we're in the same stage now," he said. "There is a massive trust factor there."

Amrita Bhasin, co-founder and CEO of a sustainable supply chain startup called Sotira, said she has been using OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini to help save time finding apparel and beauty products, especially from brands she might not know about. But she still prefers to complete the purchase herself.

"I think the process of actually buying is not super complicated," she said. "Figuring out what to buy is where I face severe decision fatigue."

Like Mandelos, she still has concerns about an agent purchasing the wrong thing or making another mistake for which she is then accountable. Most of the e-commerce sites she uses, like Amazon, have already developed incredibly fast, easy checkout processes that still leave her in control, she said.

The shopping trolley problem

For now, it's more important for agents to improve the product discovery experience than to complete transactions, said Xavier Starkloff, co-founder and CEO of AI-powered shopping platform Joko.

It's not wildly different from how shoppers have been using chatbots and assistants over the last few years, but agents can take that role much further by drawing on more data sources, more interactions, and more time, he said.

"Agentic is definitely a game changer at a time like Black Friday because it's all about finding the right deals," he added.

For retailers, a bad agentic experience could undermine years or decades of investment in establishing trust with customers, Kantar's Logan said.

Walmart and Amazon are handling this in opposing ways, with Walmart rolling out a suite of tools to make agentic shopping easier and Amazon blocking external bots in favor of having shoppers use Alexa.

Other retailers have yet to take a side regarding third-party AI agents. Target CEO Michael Fiddelke and Home Depot's head of online experiences each told Business Insider their companies are focusing their AI strategies on delivering the best experience for customers.

Logan said the hesitancy to use AI agents reminds her of shoppers' initial reluctance to use another technology that has become an indispensable retail fixture: the shopping cart.

"They had to start putting people out there with the carts, pushing them around in order to get other people to start using them. And I think that just tells you exactly how it has to be with agentic," she said.

It's the thought — and the prompt — that counts

For gift-givers, the emotional elements are more nuanced.

Setting aside the current technical performance and reliability of AI agents, holiday shopping presents a host of social and experiential considerations that could complicate a person's willingness to delegate their list to a bot.

For one thing, holiday shopping is not simply restocking the pantry with the same basics — it's a weeks-long festive event.

And then there are the different gift situations that require thoughtful personalization: A trendy present for a co-worker or neighbor carries far less weight than something special for a loved one. How would each person feel if they found out that their gift was outsourced to AI?

Bhasin said she's planning to use her agents to help her wrangle this year's holiday gift list by finding items at specific retailers both online and in-store, especially those places where she can take care of multiple presents at once.

Mandelos said he sees two sides to the question. At first blush, using AI might seem like a low-effort way to check a box. In reality, however, he says finding a truly distinctive gift is likely to involve a great deal of prompting, which could be its own kind of 21st-century love language.

To try out the tech, Mandelos is giving his agent detailed prompts and a strict budget to find gifts for friends.

For his sister's gift, he's finding it the traditional way.

content_html_zh:
The first agentic AI Black Friday is off to a rocky start

作者：Dominick Reuter 您目前正在关注该作者！ Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-22T12:10:01.258Z

When Dean Mandelos wanted to find a holiday gift for his sister, he turned to his handy new personal AI agent, Muse.

The bot, which Meta launched in September, had already helped the 29-year-old therapist in New York City list and sell a few items on eBay. It had also dutifully gathered and organized multiple bids from contractors for a door replacement job, so he figured it might be useful in finding something unique for his sister who loves to cook. Muse recommended a set of knives.

"I think that it was giving some good ideas. I just think that the thing that AI consistently misses is, like, the social aspect," Mandelos said. "My first thought would have been that it would suggest a cookbook or something. But instead, it went right towards actual tools and equipment."

Beyond more utilitarian recommendations, Mandelos also said his Muse agent encountered other hiccups in its shopping journey, from listings that had expired or sold out, to outright blocks from major e-commerce sites like Amazon and eBay.

"I would like to let it do its own thing," he said. "I need to have a reason to trust it more."

This year is the first holiday season since the release of easy-to-use AI agents to the general public. While the tools can act like personal assistants for many, it remains to be seen whether people will actually trust them to handle the annual ritual of shopping for loved ones, a deeply personal experience for many.

Mandelos' experience highlights a conundrum: the use of AI agents collides with established habits of both retailers and shoppers. While an AI bot could handle many people's holiday gift lists, it may take time before bots are trusted and empowered to truly take on the job by both consumers and retailers.

"It's the first Black Friday that AI can really play a meaningful role for sure, but it's not fully autonomous yet," said Kantar retail analyst Gina Logan. "Two-thirds of shoppers are using AI for shopping at least sometimes, but over half still prefer to control their own shopping decisions."

Early and slow adoption

For all the fanfare from marketers about the arrival of agentic commerce, there's little evidence that shoppers are handing off checkout to bots.

A Bain & Co. analysis this week of Similarweb data found that AI assistants represent less than 1% of retailers' web traffic. DoorDash and Uber also recently said that very few of their customers are using agents. Of about 320 million Uber transactions in the final week of October, only about 500 were from AI agents.

That said, adoption is rising fast, and the Bain report finds AI search is almost twice as effective as traditional web search at ultimately converting to a sale.

Abhishek Bora, head of growth at streetwear retailer All Star Elite, told Business Insider that agentic traffic accounts for about 1% of his website traffic, mostly from Meta's Muse. It's also unclear to him whether those agents are actually making a purchase or simply finding items for customers to click "buy" on.

"Once a week or twice a week we get a Muse purchase," he said. "It's small, but we have been optimizing for it."

For Bora, that means adding machine-readable data layers to All Star Elite's website that help a bot better navigate and understand the products and promotions the company offers.

The 1% figure also appears in a survey from the consumer insights platform Zappi, which found that 1% of respondents mentioned — without prompting — that they use AI to shop.

Steve Phillips, the firm's founder and chief innovation officer, said these agentic one percenters generally skewed younger, wealthier, and more tech-savvy.

"That's not unusual for any sort of tech. They would be the first people buying Apple phones," he said.

Phillips likened the uptake of agentic shopping to the first days of booking hotels on the internet in the early dot-com era. Travelers would search the web for a room and then pick up the phone to make a reservation.

"No one was booking online, but people were using the web, and I think we're in the same stage now," he said. "There is a massive trust factor there."

Amrita Bhasin, co-founder and CEO of a sustainable supply chain startup called Sotira, said she has been using OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini to help save time finding apparel and beauty products, especially from brands she might not know about. But she still prefers to complete the purchase herself.

"I think the process of actually buying is not super complicated," she said. "Figuring out what to buy is where I face severe decision fatigue."

Like Mandelos, she still has concerns about an agent purchasing the wrong thing or making another mistake for which she is then accountable. Most of the e-commerce sites she uses, like Amazon, have already developed incredibly fast, easy checkout processes that still leave her in control, she said.

The shopping trolley problem

For now, it's more important for agents to improve the product discovery experience than to complete transactions, said Xavier Starkloff, co-founder and CEO of AI-powered shopping platform Joko.

It's not wildly different from how shoppers have been using chatbots and assistants over the last few years, but agents can take that role much further by drawing on more data sources, more interactions, and more time, he said.

"Agentic is definitely a game changer at a time like Black Friday because it's all about finding the right deals," he added.

For retailers, a bad agentic experience could undermine years or decades of investment in establishing trust with customers, Kantar's Logan said.

Walmart and Amazon are handling this in opposing ways, with Walmart rolling out a suite of tools to make agentic shopping easier and Amazon blocking external bots in favor of having shoppers use Alexa.

Other retailers have yet to take a side regarding third-party AI agents. Target CEO Michael Fiddelke and Home Depot's head of online experiences each told Business Insider their companies are focusing their AI strategies on delivering the best experience for customers.

Logan said the hesitancy to use AI agents reminds her of shoppers' initial reluctance to use another technology that has become an indispensable retail fixture: the shopping cart.

"They had to start putting people out there with the carts, pushing them around in order to get other people to start using them. And I think that just tells you exactly how it has to be with agentic," she said.

It's the thought — and the prompt — that counts

For gift-givers, the emotional elements are more nuanced.

Setting aside the current technical performance and reliability of AI agents, holiday shopping presents a host of social and experiential considerations that could complicate a person's willingness to delegate their list to a bot.

For one thing, holiday shopping is not simply restocking the pantry with the same basics — it's a weeks-long festive event.

And then there are the different gift situations that require thoughtful personalization: A trendy present for a co-worker or neighbor carries far less weight than something special for a loved one. How would each person feel if they found out that their gift was outsourced to AI?

Bhasin said she's planning to use her agents to help her wrangle this year's holiday gift list by finding items at specific retailers both online and in-store, especially those places where she can take care of multiple presents at once.

Mandelos said he sees two sides to the question. At first blush, using AI might seem like a low-effort way to check a box. In reality, however, he says finding a truly distinctive gift is likely to involve a great deal of prompting, which could be its own kind of 21st-century love language.

To try out the tech, Mandelos is giving his agent detailed prompts and a strict budget to find gifts for friends.

For his sister's gift, he's finding it the traditional way.
